name: Tomas Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and have handled calls and chats at the contact centre for years. I finished secondary school and am about as good at this work as most experienced agents. I earn the usual rate. I use AI every day to sort long chat histories, then open the original account before I answer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Anya, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. She works a library desk, and we have about four months of expenses saved. A few other centres are near us. I like getting a wrong fee removed while the customer is still on the line; I dislike when the dashboard rewards a fast close that makes somebody call again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau sounds like the history sorter I already use: a quick way to find a page, not a final answer. I would ask colleagues to check the original fee before closing a chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job remains, but four months saved does not make a mortgage cheap. Anya’s library pay helps, yet both wages keep the children’s routine steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking calls and using the sorter with the account open. In the first year of small change, I’d save the cost of two bought coffees a week and bring wrong summary examples to our staff group for a shared error list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about bills, calm about the tool itself. A fast close is no saving when the customer calls back about the same wrong fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the wrong summaries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remove customer names and show the staff group the fee line the summary missed. One example is an anecdote; ten of the same error is something we can ask management to count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that saving buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anya (my partner) and I would put the coffee money in the mortgage account after payday. It is small, but I would rather see the number grow than assume it will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take standard replies first, and we should compare paid hours with repeat calls before declaring a saving. I would join the staff group’s request for those figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ordinary calls could shrink enough to put my own hours at risk, even though I use the tools well. Four months saved lets me search, but another centre may automate the same queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d test the new answer checker on twenty old billing cases during paid time and log wrong fees. In the first year routine replies move, I’d join the staff group request for monthly hours and apply for a posted paid audit-support role only if its offered wage and hours cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Knowing how to use a tool does not mean a company needs the same number of agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask another agent to check five of the disputed cases without my notes. If our counts differ, I would fix the test before bringing the figures to the group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you study audit work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for a course just because a poster says audit is the future. I would take employer-funded training on paid time if a posted paid job required it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could answer and check almost any call we handle. I would ask the staff group to seek written notice and posted paid roles before the rota changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think cheap thinking AI could take most of my desk in 2028. Robots around 2031 do not extend my headset job, and four months of savings would go quickly under the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help the group write a notice request and stop plans for a new patio set. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid billing-review role only if offered wage and hours cover our mortgage, and take funded training only if a named vacancy requires it on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Four months of mortgage money is time to search, not a second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about the patio set?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Anya (my partner) the patio furniture can wait. We can keep the cash for the mortgage and school costs without losing anything essential.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would ask for notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff group to send the same notice question for every shift. A private answer to me would not protect colleagues whose calls disappear on another rota.

I’d demand **posted paid roles** before 2028 cuts.

I see **four months saved** as a short search window.
do: Join a **group notice request** and defer patio spending in 2026.

Take a funded **course** on paid time only if the named posted opening requires it.
S2.quote: Four months of mortgage money is time to search, not a second career.
fieldNote: He knows **2028 thinking AI** is the relevant call deadline.
He would delay **patio furniture** to preserve cash.
He asks for **funded study** only when a named vacancy requires it.

steps.text: Join staff group written notice request covering every shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to find out whether audit work is a real paid job. I would ask the staff group to see the posted wage and training plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn to check difficult automated decisions by 2031, but full AGI might do that work too. Four months saved lets me test a route only while the current wage continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take a funded audit course on paid time only if a posted paid role requires it, and help the staff group check its terms. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for that role only if the written offered wage and hours cover our mortgage; otherwise I’d keep paid calls while searching nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with time to test the job. A course without a posted audit wage is a map with no destination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the quality agent to show me three wrong automated charges during paid training. If the course is just a video, I would not count it as evidence that I can do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would Anya need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Anya (my partner) the offered hours as well as the hourly rate. A higher rate for half the week could leave the mortgage short.

I’d seek a **group review** of paid course terms.

I know **full AGI** may reach audit work too.

fieldNote: He wants **real wrong charges** during training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives workers a decade to ask for honest annual staffing figures and paid learning. I would help the staff group keep that request alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could still earn for years and add to savings, though full thinking AI may take calls in 2036. Robots arrive around 2039, later than my screen risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking calls, add a fixed amount to the mortgage reserve and help the staff group request yearly paid-hour figures. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a posted paid audit role only if my calls fall and the written wage and hours cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, but the house is not in danger this month. A decade before AGI in 2036 gives me time to save without assuming the calls will stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which number matters annually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the number of paid agents and hours, not only the number of customers answered. A faster system can hide a smaller payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the family move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children in their school unless Anya (my partner) and I had a signed offer and an affordable route. A job title in another town is not enough.

I’d seek **paid learning** before 2036 calls change.

I know **2036 thinking AI** may still take calls.
do: Keep **taking calls**, save monthly and seek group hour figures from 2026.
Apply for **posted audit work** after 2036 if calls fall and pay covers mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work, stable at present.
S4.quote: A faster system can hide a smaller payroll.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the calls and checking I know could move to cheap thinking AI in two years. Four months saved is a search window, not a wage. Written notice, a posted paid audit opening with mortgage-covering hours and paid training would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who counts a second call after a wrong answer. The first automated answer looks cheap only if nobody counts the customer coming back angry.

headlineQuote: The first automated answer looks cheap only if nobody counts the customer coming back angry.
portrait: At **43**, Tomas is an experienced average-skill agent after secondary school on typical pay.
He and Anya support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with four months saved.

He seeks **group evidence** and paid audit work as routine answers move to software.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his screen work before he secures another mortgage-covering wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a posted paid audit opening and paid training would help.
